assessment.nobel_worthiness: The credit-cycles model shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a foundational mechanism in modern macro-finance and shapes how financial crises and policy are analysed. Its influence on theory, quantitative macro and policy is broad and durable.
assessment.attribution: The core contribution is the Kiyotaki–Moore dynamic collateral-constraint model. Credit for it is cleanly concentrated in these two. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the related financial-accelerator and empirical strand, but the financial-accelerator framework has already been recognised in earlier prizes. I keep the laureate list to the two originators.
assessment.maturity: The central paper dates from 1997, with nearly three decades of confirmation, extension and use in quantitative and policy models, including after 2008. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: How the Committee weighs this against earlier recognition of financial-frictions work.
Whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be added; I judge the case for the two originators stronger.
I have not independently verified citation or impact figures.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work changed how economists and policymakers understand technology, trade exposure and labour-market adjustment. It combines the task-based view of technological change with credible empirical identification of the local effects of import competition, and it has reshaped the debate on inequality and trade policy.
assessment.attribution: The task-based approach and the trade-shock empirics are separable strands, shared among several authors (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz). Autor is central to both strands and Hanson to the trade-shock work. I propose these two as the most defensible pair, with Dorn and Katz as plausible alternatives. The pairing involves judgement.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly two decades; the China-shock papers date from about 2013–2016. The long-run effects are well documented, though some interpretations remain debated.
uncertainties: Attribution is genuinely contested among four credited names and the three-person limit forces a choice.
Debate persists over the magnitude and persistence of the trade-shock effects and how well they generalise.
Related prior and parallel work (for example on skill-biased technological change) may complicate credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run historical series on top incomes and wealth built a new empirical base for inequality research and public debate, with major influence on tax and distribution policy research. The data-construction contribution is substantial and durable.
assessment.attribution: The top-income series are principally Piketty and Saez, with Zucman prominent on wealth and offshore holdings. Zucman is arguably earlier in career. I propose the established pair, noting the case for Zucman is real but less mature.
assessment.maturity: The foundational top-income work dates from the early 2000s and is widely replicated and extended. Later wealth and theory claims are more contested.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over wealth-tax and capital-share interpretations and some data-construction choices.
Policy salience may make evaluation contentious.
Overlap with Saez's other credited work (B014) may split credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework and the associated theory of monetary policy underlie how central banks analyse and conduct policy. Their impact on both academic macroeconomics and institutions is very large.
assessment.attribution: The credited set is very large (eight names) and the contributions are layered: nominal-rigidity microfoundations, estimated DSGE models, policy rules, and the normative theory of monetary policy. I select Woodford (theoretical synthesis and normative policy), Gali (the canonical framework) and Taylor (the policy rule). This is an unavoidably debatable cut, and Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets all have strong claims.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly 30 years and has been tested through several policy regimes, including the post-2008 and post-2020 inflation episodes. Mature, though the post-2020 inflation episode renewed scrutiny of some models.
uncertainties: The three-person limit makes the laureate choice arbitrary relative to the contribution.
Methodological critiques of DSGE models since the financial crisis.
Recognition overlaps with earlier prizes in macroeconomics and monetary theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data was used to measure intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation, and to estimate neighbourhood effects. This opened a large empirical agenda in public and labour economics and has had considerable policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure across the mobility atlas and related work, and Hendren is prominent in the neighbourhood-effects and causal-place work. Friedman and Katz are also credited. I propose the pair with the clearest individual leadership.
assessment.maturity: The main results are roughly 10–12 years old. Replication and follow-up are substantial but the long-run policy validation is still emerging.
uncertainties: Relatively recent; the committee may prefer more time for confirmation.
Some methodological debate on measurement and on causal interpretation of place effects.
Chetty's work also appears in B014, which could affect how credit is distributed across ballots.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for estimating demand with differentiated products and dynamic industry models turned industrial organisation into a quantitative, empirically grounded field. They are also used in antitrust, merger review and trade analysis, giving them wide applied reach.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand framework is attributable to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also made distinct contributions on dynamic games and estimation. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin have real contributions but are more peripheral to the core method.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995 and is the standard tool, with long confirmation. Maturity is strong.
uncertainties: Relative weight of methodological versus substantive contributions.
Overlap with other empirical-IO credit (Bresnahan, Reiss) complicates the laureate set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formal models of present bias, self-control problems and reference dependence extended behavioural economics into tractable theory with applications to savings, contracts and policy design. The contribution is substantial, but behavioural economics has already been recognised by earlier prizes.
assessment.attribution: Laibson is central on quasi-hyperbolic discounting and its macro and savings applications. Rabin is central on formal behavioural theory, including reference dependence and projection. Koszegi, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue also have significant claims, so the choice is a judgement.
assessment.maturity: The theory is 20–30 years old, with extensive experimental and field evidence and policy adoption, for example of default-based savings. Mature.
uncertainties: Marginal contribution relative to earlier behavioural recognition.
Mixed evidence on stability and magnitude of some behavioural parameters.
Attribution is spread over five credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting changed the theory and empirics of trade, shifting attention from countries and industries to firms and the reallocation channel of gains from trade. It has had a lasting influence on the field.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the central contribution, and Helpman is a leading contributor to the wider new-trade and heterogeneous-firm literature. Redding has major contributions to quantitative and spatial trade. The trade field has already been recognised through Krugman's prize, and some credit for quantitative trade is also in B001.
assessment.maturity: The framework dates from 2003 and has had two decades of extensive testing and extension, so maturity is good.
uncertainties: Overlap with other trade ballots (B001, B043) splits the field's credit and could dilute support.
Whether the Committee treats Melitz's contribution as sufficiently distinct from earlier trade-theory recognition.
